Mathematics emerged in the fertile river valley between the Tigris and Euphrates (modern Iraq) among the Sumerians, who established the world's first urban civilizations around 3500–3000 BCE. The Sumerians developed cuneiform writing—wedge-shaped marks pressed into wet clay tablets—which became the medium for the earliest surviving mathematical records. Successive peoples—Akkadians, Babylonians, and Assyrians—inherited and extended this tradition over nearly three millennia.

#### The Sexagesimal System
The most distinctive feature of Mesopotamian mathematics was its **base-60 (sexagesimal) place-value numeral system**, fully developed by the Old Babylonian period (c. 1900–1600 BCE). Unlike the additive systems of Egypt, the Babylonian system was genuinely positional: the value of a symbol depended on its position, much like our modern decimal system. This is why we still divide the hour into 60 minutes, the minute into 60 seconds, and the circle into 360 degrees—direct inheritances from Babylonian mathematics.

The Babylonians used two basic symbols: a vertical wedge for units (1–9) and a horizontal wedge for tens (10–50). Because their system lacked a consistent symbol for zero in its earliest form (a placeholder symbol appeared only later, around the Seleucid period), ambiguity could arise, resolved by context.
